STAGE 01

Regression models

Can linear and tree models turn recent momentum into a better-than-benchmark long/flat strategy?

regression_models_comparison.ipynb · logistic_regression.ipynb · lasso_regression.ipynb
01 · overview

Five models, one question: will a stock rise tomorrow?

Inputs: 1-, 5-, 15- and 20-day returns of every S&P 500 stock since 2000. The first 70% of dates train the models; the last 30% test them.

Strategy: each day, hold the stocks a model favours; stay in cash otherwise. Compare with holding every stock equally.

Cross-validation runs in date order, so no model trains on the future.

ModelPredictsGoes long when
Linear regressionnext-day returnforecast > 0
Lassonext-day returnforecast > 0
Logistic regressionchance of an up dayabove 50%
Decision treechance of an up dayabove 50%
Tuned decision treechance of an up dayabove 50%
01 · results

No model beat the benchmark; Lasso came closest

What it shows: how $1 grew from Sep 2018 under each strategy (top), how far each fell from its peak (middle), and returns by calendar year (bottom). Grey dotted is the equal-weighted S&P 500 benchmark.

  • Growth: benchmark about $3.45; Lasso about $3.27, logistic and linear about $3.10–3.15, tuned tree about $2.93. The unpruned tree trailed far behind at about $1.97.
  • Downturns: all fell 35–40% in March 2020. In 2022 the strategies lost about 4–6% against the benchmark's 10%, because they sat in cash on some down days.
  • Best single year: the tuned tree's 2020, about 37% against the benchmark's 21%.

regression_models_comparison.ipynb · section 5 · your run

01 · accuracy and lessons

Barely better than a coin flip, so time in the market decided the results

MetricLinearLassoLogisticDecision treeTuned tree
TypeRegressionRegressionClassifierClassifierClassifier
Hit rate52.0%52.1%52.0%50.1%51.5%
ROC-AUC0.5090.5090.5100.5010.509
Rank IC0.0200.0200.0220.0010.014
Time long86%90%84%51%69%

What it shows: out-of-sample skill for each model. Hit rate is how often it called the direction right; ROC-AUC and rank IC measure how well it ranked up days above down days (0.5 and 0 mean no skill); time long is the share of stock-days it held. regression_models_comparison.ipynb · section 4 · your run

  • Skill was tiny: hit rates of 50–52% and AUCs of 0.50–0.51. Daily direction is mostly noise.
  • Lasso came closest to the benchmark because it stayed long 90% of the time, not because it predicted better.
  • The unpruned tree had no skill (AUC 0.5005, IC near 0) and was long only half the time, hence its $1.97.
  • Next: look deeper at one stock's own history: trend, bands, momentum and volatility.
STAGE 02

Time-series features

Turn AAPL's price history into the signals a trading agent can see: trend, bands, momentum and volatility.

time_series.ipynb · AAPL, March 2020 to August 2024
02 · trend

AAPL rose 240% with price above its 50-day average 62% of the time

What it shows: daily close (white) with the 20-day (blue) and 50-day (pink dashed) moving averages, Mar 2020 to Aug 2024; the shading is the gap between them. The averages crossed 25 times. Wide gaps mark trends, such as the 2020 rally and mid-2024 surge; tight crossings mark choppy stretches, such as most of 2022. time_series.ipynb · your run

02 · volatility bands

Price closed outside its Bollinger Bands on 10% of days

What it shows: the daily close (white) inside a purple band set two standard deviations either side of its 20-day average. It balloons in fast markets (the 2020 run-up, 2022 swings, mid-2024 surge) and pinches in calm ones. Closes outside it, about 1 day in 10, flag unusually strong moves. time_series.ipynb · your run

02 · momentum, volatility and volume

Volatility spiked above 100% in March 2020, then mostly stayed between 15% and 30%

What it shows: three of the agent's inputs, from top to bottom.

  • Volatility (annualized, 20-day): over 100% in the March 2020 crash, flare-ups to about 50–55% in late 2020 and 2022, and mostly 15–30% since 2023.
  • RSI: above 70 (overbought, red zone) on 11% of days and below 30 (oversold, green zone) on just 1%, the signature of a long uptrend.
  • Volume: heaviest in 2020, often 200–400M shares a day; usually under 100M since 2023.

02 · handoff

Seven features become the agent's view of the market

Saved for the agent

AAPL_trading_features.csv: Close, 20- and 50-day averages, price volatility, upper and lower Bollinger Bands, RSI. 1,124 trading days.

  • Trend: where price sits against its averages.
  • Extremes: band breaks and RSI zones.
  • Risk: how volatile the stock has been lately.

STAGE 03

RL trading agent

A deep Q-network learns when to buy, sell or hold AAPL from the stage-2 features, then trades a period it has never seen.

rl_trading_agent.ipynb · trained Mar 2020 to Apr 2023, tested Apr 2023 to Aug 2024
03 · overview

The agent sees the market and its own position, and learns from daily P&L

Sees

Daily changes in the seven features, plus how many shares it holds and whether they are in profit.

Does

Hold, buy one share (up to five), or sell the oldest share. Impossible actions are blocked; costs of 5 basis points apply.

Learns from

Each day's mark-to-market profit or loss, through experience replay over five training passes (episodes).

Earlier versions bought every day and never sold. Showing the agent its own position, rewarding daily P&L and pacing exploration fixed that.

03 · lessons

A stock-only agent mostly learns to ride the trend

  • It learned something, but not enough: the final model had the smallest drawdown ($64 vs $163 for buy-and-hold) yet earned less than random trading. Its episode 2 model came within $7 of buy-and-hold.
  • But buy-and-hold won in a market that rose steadily. With only "buy" and "sell", the best policy in a bull run is close to holding.
  • The environment matters as much as the network: position awareness, the right reward and paced exploration were what made it trade at all.
  • Next: give the agent instruments that pay in more kinds of market. Options can profit from rises, falls and calm, if they are priced well.
STAGE 04

GBM options RL agent

The agent now prices options with a geometric Brownian motion model, forecasts volatility, and buys and sells SPY calls and puts under margin rules.

gbm_options_rl_agent.ipynb
04 · overview

From a price model to priced trades

1 · Model the price

Geometric Brownian motion: steady drift plus random shocks that grow with the price.

2 · Forecast volatility

Five forecasters (historical, EWMA, GARCH, HAR, VIX) scored on the next 21 days.

3 · Find the edge

Compare what the model expects an option to pay with what the market charges.

4 · Trade

Six actions: hold, buy or sell calls and puts, close. One-month at-the-money contracts.

5 · Control risk

Bid/ask costs, margin on short options, forced buy-backs and a crash filter.

6 · Track every trade

Entry, exit, Greeks, edge and P&L for each of the four position types.

04 · the price model

GBM fans outcomes wider over time and skews them upward

What it shows: 20,000 simulated one-year paths from $100 (8% drift, 20% volatility). Ninety percent end between $76 and $148. The ending prices lean right: the mean ($108) sits above the median ($106) and 38% of paths still lose money. The notebook then checks where real markets break this model: fatter tails and crashes. func_lib GBM simulator

04 · what it can trade

Buyers risk only the premium; sellers keep at most the premium

What it shows: the agent's four positions, priced with Black-Scholes. Buyers lose at most the premium ($224 call, $191 put); sellers keep it in calm markets, but a 10% drop costs a put seller $809. That is why selling comes with margin and a crash filter. func_lib Black-Scholes pricer

04 · volatility forecasts

Options were usually priced for more volatility than arrived

  • Top: HAR-RV (blue), GARCH (pink) and VIX (green) forecasts of the next 21 days' volatility against what happened (white), 2010–2026. All three track the spikes: 2011, 2015, the 2020 crash near 100%, and early 2025.
  • Bottom: implied minus realized volatility. Implied was higher on 85% of days, by 3.8 points on average.
  • Why it matters: that gap is the premium option sellers collect, and the reason the agent may sell.

gbm_options_rl_agent.ipynb · section 3 · your run

04 · lessons

Options add pricing, risk and realism to the agent's job

  • Implied volatility usually runs above realized volatility: buying options tends to overpay; selling collects a premium for bearing crash risk.
  • The edge is mostly a view on drift and volatility, so the drift assumption is the most important setting.
  • Risk controls shape the result: margin, a cap on short positions and a crash filter decide whether selling survives a bad month.
  • Every number reconciles: account equity equals the sum of trade profits to the cent, and pricing matches independent checks.
Supporting project · portfolio construction

Risk parity grew $1 to about $1.61; equal weight reached about $2.36

Idea: weight S&P 500, gold and 10-year Treasury futures so each adds similar risk, which means more weight in calm bonds.

  • Top: growth of $1, risk parity (blue) vs equal weight (pink), 2015–2025.
  • Bottom: drawdowns. Both fell about 12% in March 2020 and about 16% in 2022.
  • Why it lagged: 2022 hit bonds as hard as stocks, the case risk parity handles worst, and equal weight held more of the gold and stock rally since 2023.

Where it goes next

Next steps

  • Size the risk parity book with a volatility target, so its lower risk can be levered up to match returns.
  • Steadier agents: Double DQN, risk-aware rewards, several seeds and a validation split.
  • Real option prices: option-chain data with the volatility smile.
  • Richer models: stochastic volatility (Heston) and jumps for pricing.
  • Defined-risk trades: spreads that cap a short position's loss.
  • Combine the pieces: use risk parity to size the options book alongside other strategies.
